newsitem.title: CANADA: Potash Corp sees volumes boosting prices.
newsitem.headline: Potash Corp sees volumes boosting prices.

text.p: Potash Corp of Saskatchewan Inc said on Thursday its improved second-quarter earnings were attributable to the addition of PCS nitrogen for the full quarter along with higher potash and phosphate sales volumes, which were favourably affected by a one of the best-ever North American spring seasons.
Potash Corp said the strong volumes so far in 1997 should result in higher prices going forward.
During the quarter the Company produced 12 percent more potash than during the second quarter of 1996 but ended the quarter with inventories 31 percent lower than a year ago.

"These record earnings...demonstrate the benefit of our acquisition strategy for our shareholders. Our diversified product line successfully integrates the production and sale of our three primary nutrients creating a balanced corporate earnings profile," Potash Chairman and Chief Executive Chuck Childers said in a statement.

He said the world economic and agricultural outlook is bright and world grain stocks remain at historically low levels, while stong economic growth continues to pull the demand of meat and grain along with it.

"Our three major export markets, China, India and Brazil, are continuing to import our products. These market conditions are enhanced by our firm supply situation as we are entering the new fertilizer year with low or manageable inventories in all our products and our operations functioning well," Childers said.
He said the company has a domestic potash price increase slated for this fall and is hopeful the current DAP environment will create upward pricing pressure.
Childers said Potash Corp's flexibility in product selection and choice of markets will benefit the company in the second half of the year.

"Approximately 40 percent of our gross margin in each of phosphate and nitrogen comes from the non-fertilizer side of the business. This diversification illustrates our ability to weather temporary glitches in the fertilizer markets," Childers said.
